question: Did the game end at the right time, or did it overstay/undershoot?

seats.persona: an experienced boardgamer who compares everything to games they know
an impatient player who wants every turn to matter
a competitive player who hunts for the strongest line every turn
a cautious first-timer who plays what the rules literally say

answers:
**PLAY_AGAIN:** YES

The core concept works—deduction with asymmetric roles (Locksmith vs Crackers), information hidden in an arrangement, and the time-pressure scoring (12 turns for a full payout) creates meaningful tension. This is solid

The game ended before anyone took a turn. A round that never starts teaches nothing about design—you can't evaluate decisions that were never made, and players sitting idle waiting for a move that never came is just broken, not a game.
The game ended before play began—I was waiting on the Locksmith's opening move and never took a turn. No gameplay happened to evaluate whether the game's length or pacing worked.

Undershoot. The game ended before any turn was taken — we never got out of the starting position. For a 4-round game, ending at round 1 with zero choices made doesn't feel like a real game, just a false start.

confusion_events.why: turn budget spent at 1 moves — game unfinished; verdicts taken from the position reached
